title: He wrote a telepathy novel and accidentally summoned fans
summary:
The funniest/most revealing bit is Tyler Alterman realizing his premise hits a little too close to home: after he explains Psychofauna—2025, everyone wakes up “vibe psychic,” myths/ideologies become belief-powered entities, and culture wars turn into literal memeplex warfare—people keep replying with some version of “but our world is like that,” and Tyler’s basically like: yeah… that’s the point.

The arc starts small and earnest: on Feb 13, 2024, Tyler makes a birthday wish for “unfiltered reactions” to chapter one. Then it spikes hard on Apr 29 when he launches the novel as a weekly web serial and immediately posts, stunned, that he’s at 191 subscribers (and 261 the next day). Friends pile on with specific hype: Malcolm Ocean calls it “a terrifying mashup” of Understand and Nexus (even if it’s not written as horror), and puheenix straight-up tells people to “subscribe and donate” because the world is that good. Tyler does the classic creator whiplash—“you guys realize I’m just making all this up right?”—while also doing community-builder moves like offering the bonus stories free to low-income readers via DM.

Peak drama turns IRL in October: Tyler’s writing in a famous coffee shop when two moms and their kids ask about his book, buy paid subs on the spot, and later he overhears them reading it aloud—getting increasingly lost in the Jung-meets-neurosci worldbuilding (“magnetoreceptors” becomes the villain). He spirals—did they enjoy it or want a refund?—then makes a vow to make draft two “engaging and comprehensible.” By Jan 2025 he finishes the manuscript (140,500 words), asks for beta readers, and gets so many (300+) that the Google Doc becomes sluggish and he has to herd feedback into a Discord. Along the way, the model spreads: Tasshin Fogleman explicitly says he’s serializing his own novel “following Tyler’s lead.”

Why care: it’s a neat case study in how an internet micro-scene turns a weird, theory-drenched fiction concept into an actual audience—and then forces the author to confront the real boss fight of creative work: not writing the wild thing, but making the wild thing legible to normal humans who just wanted a fun book to read with their kid.
